title: Illustrations of the IPA: Thai
authors: Tingsabadh, M. R. Kalaya; Abramson, Arthur S.
key_findings: Standard Thai has five tones: high, mid, low, rising, falling (khaa mid 'to get stuck', khàa 'galangal', khâa 'I', kháa 'to trade', khǎa 'leg').
Nine vowel qualities; length is distinctive for all vowels.
Only /p t k ʔ m n ŋ w j/ occur syllable-finally; final /p t ʔ/ have no audible release.
Primary stress falls on the final syllable of a word; the last primary stress before the end of a major prosodic group commonly takes extra stress.
/r/ vs /l/ distinction is not robust; many speakers favour [l] for single initial r; as second element of clusters both /l/ and /r/ tend to be deleted.
In polysyllabic words, low and high tones on short-/a/ glottal-stop syllables become mid when unstressed, with loss of the glottal stop.
practical_applications: Lengthen/emphasise the LAST syllable of a word, not the first, when directing emphasis in Thai VO.
Unreleased final stops: a TTS that releases -p/-t/-k sounds foreign.
Do not force tones on unstressed กระ-/ประ-/สะ- prefixes.
limitations: Only pp. 25-26 (vowels, tones, stress, conventions) were read from the scanned PDF; p. 24 and pp. 27-28 not read.
Describes careful Standard (Bangkok) Thai, not regional varieties.

title: Lexical tone and sentence prosody in Thai
key_findings: Tones divide into 'dynamic' (falling, rising: rapid F0 movement) and 'static' (high, mid, low: slow movements).
Citation forms are the 'ideal' tone shapes; in running speech neighbouring tones cause coarticulation (e.g. first of two falling tones falls less far).
Certain unstressed CV syllables with short /a/ are normally toneless or neutralised to mid in running speech.
Three terminal junctures: rising (surprise, doubt, question), sustained (syntactic breaks, final syllable prolonged) and falling (sentence ends).
Sentence-final particles are prime carriers of terminal junctures; their 'lexical' tone is often overridden by sentence intonation (following Henderson 1949).
Sentence accent = syllable lengthening + tone contour approaching the ideal shape + amplitude increase.
practical_applications: Put attitude/question melody on the final particle, not on content words.
Sentence-final content words drop lower in F0: a TTS that keeps a full high 'citation' fall on the last word sounds read-aloud.
Emphasis = length + clear tone shape + loudness, not raised pitch.
limitations: Small corpus (one dialogue, one monologue), mostly auditory; author calls observations preliminary.
Pages 380-385 read; final page with Table 2 and conclusions not read.

title: Using stress to disambiguate spoken Thai sentences containing syntactic ambiguity
authors: Potisuk, Siripong; Harper, Mary P.; Gandour, Jack
key_findings: Stress in connected Thai classified from rhyme duration, mean F0, F0 SD, mean energy and energy SD.
Rhyme duration is a better correlate of stress than nucleus or whole syllable.
Monosyllabic content words are strongly stressed; grammatical words/clitics are weakly stressed unless emphasised.
A bisyllabic noun compound has weak-strong stress, a subject-verb sequence strong-strong: stress disambiguates structure.
practical_applications: Particles and function words (ก็, ที่, ของ, จะ) should be light in VO; content words carry weight.
Compound nouns (e.g. แว่นตา, สายตา) read weak-strong; reading them strong-strong can change parsing.
limitations: Five speakers, read lab sentences; classifier accuracy dropped with speaker-independent normalisation.

title: Intonation in Thai (in Hirst & Di Cristo, eds., Intonation Systems: A Survey of Twenty Languages, pp. 376-394)
key_findings: Per secondary summaries: three intonation classes in Thai - Fall (finality), Rise (non-finality/question) and Convoluted (contrariness, emphasis) - superimposed on the five lexical tones.
Builds on the author's 1983 Edinburgh PhD thesis 'Intonation in Thai'.
practical_applications: Use three melody labels (fall / rise / convoluted) in voice direction rather than English-style pitch accents.
limitations: Not read; findings come only from search snippets and a computational paper (Charnvivit et al. 2003) that uses the classes.

title: F0 feature extraction by polynomial regression function for monosyllabic Thai tone recognition / intonation pattern recognition (Eurospeech 2003, co-author Luksaneeyanawin)
key_findings: States there are three classes of intonation pattern in Thai: Fall, Rise and Convolution.
practical_applications: Supports the three-class intonation vocabulary for voice direction.
limitations: Only the search snippet was seen; exact title not confirmed.

title: Interaction between tone and intonation in Thai after unilateral brain damage
key_findings: Tones in sentence-final position were significantly lower in F0 than in sentence-initial or -medial position, for normal and brain-damaged speakers.
practical_applications: Expect and allow final lowering; do not 'correct' a TTS that lowers the last word as long as the tone shape is kept.
limitations: Search summary only; sample and clinical focus not checked.

title: Anticipatory tonal coarticulation in Thai noun compounds after unilateral brain damage
authors: Gandour, Jack; Ponglorpisit, S.; Dechongkit, S.; et al.
key_findings: Brain and Language 45:1-20: the falling tone's pitch height and slope were affected by the following tone (anticipatory coarticulation) in noun compounds.
practical_applications: Tone shapes in compounds legitimately differ from citation forms; judge a TTS by whether the word is recognisable, not by matching citation contours.
limitations: Search summary only.

title: Tone features, tone perception, and peak alignment in Thai (as summarised in a citing source)
key_findings: Per a citing source: any actual rise in the high tone is optional in citation form and prohibited in connected speech.
practical_applications: A rising 'high' tone in running speech can be misheard; high tone in connected speech should be high-level/peak late.
limitations: Only the search snippet from a citing document was seen.

title: The Vowels and Tones of Standard Thai: Acoustical Measurements and Experiments (IJAL 28(2), part 3; Indiana Univ. Research Center Publication 20)
key_findings: Foundational acoustic and synthetic-speech perception study of Thai vowels and tones; based on 1960 Columbia dissertation.
practical_applications: Baseline reference for tone shapes and vowel length.
limitations: Bibliographic record only; measurements not read.

title: หลักเกณฑ์การทับศัพท์ภาษาอังกฤษ (Royal Institute English transcription rules, reproduced as DLTV Thai lesson handout, Mattayom 3)
authors: Royal Institute / Office of the Royal Society (rules); DLTV handout compiler
key_findings: Vowels transcribed from the English dictionary pronunciation; consonants by a fixed table.
Silent letters take ์ (horn = ฮอร์น, world = เวิลด์).
ไม้ไต่คู้ used to distinguish from Thai words (log = ล็อก) or to show syllabification.
No tone marks in transcriptions, except where the word would clash with a Thai word (coke = โค้ก, coma = โคม่า).
Double final consonants: drop one in general words (football = ฟุตบอล) but keep both with ์ in technical terms/proper names (cell = เซลล์).
Hyphenated and open compounds are written joined (cross-stitch = ครอสสติตช์, night club = ไนต์คลับ).
Long-established loanwords in the RI dictionary keep their spelling.
practical_applications: RI spelling is a WRITTEN standard and deliberately omits tones: a TTS respelling may add tone marks (spell as said) but subtitles should keep RI/brand spelling.
limitations: Secondary reproduction in a school handout; consonant/vowel tables were referred to but the extracted text did not include them.
license: public educational document (DLTV); rules by ORST

title: หลักเกณฑ์การใช้เครื่องหมายวรรคตอนและเครื่องหมายอื่น ๆ (Office of the Royal Society page)
authors: สำนักงานราชบัณฑิตยสภา
key_findings: Per search summary of the ORST page: ฯลฯ at the end of a list is read 'ละ' or 'และอื่น ๆ'; in the middle (ก ฯลฯ ฮ) it is read 'ละถึง'.
practical_applications: Normaliser: ฯลฯ followed by more text → 'ละถึง'; at end → 'และอื่น ๆ' (or 'ละ').
limitations: The ORST page refused connection; only the search engine summary was seen. Year unknown (0).

title: ฯลฯ - วิกิพจนานุกรม
key_findings: Gives readings 'ละ' (omitting text at the end) and 'ละถึง' (omitting text in the middle); cites no source.
practical_applications: Corroborates the ORST readings.
limitations: Community source, no citations; does not list 'และอื่น ๆ'.

title: HOYA ตอกย้ำผู้นำ ตลาดเลนส์แว่นตา เปิดตัวนวัตกรรมเลนส์โปรเกรสซีฟสุดล้ำ ...
authors: Marketeer Online (press release content from ไทยโฮยา เลนซ์)
key_findings: Brand written 'HOYA (โฮยา)'; Thai company 'บริษัท ไทยโฮยา เลนซ์ จำกัด'.
Progressive lens = 'เลนส์โปรเกรสซีฟ' (one tag misspells 'โปรแกรสซีฟ').
Presbyopia = 'สายตายาวตามอายุ'; myopia = 'สายตาสั้น'; astigmatism = 'เอียง' ('สายตาสั้นและเอียง').
practical_applications: Brand-verified Thai spelling of HOYA is โฮยา (no tone mark), not โฮย่า.
limitations: Trade media rewrite of a press release; spelling of the spoken tone not shown (RI style omits tone marks).

title: เอสซีลอร์ เปิดตัวนวัตกรรมเลนส์โปรเกรสซีฟ “Varilux Comfort® Max” รุ่นล่าสุดเพื่อตอบโจทย์ชีวิตยุคนิวนอร์มอล
authors: บริษัท เอสซีลอร์ ดิสทริบิวชั่น (ประเทศไทย) จำกัด via Vivaldi Integrated PR
key_findings: Issuer is Essilor Distribution (Thailand) itself.
Thai spellings: เอสซีลอร์, เอสซีลอร์ กรุ๊ป, วารีลักส์, วารีลักส์ คอมฟอร์ต แม็กซ์, เลนส์โปรเกรสซีฟ.
Target group described as having 'ปัญหาสายตายาวตามอายุ'.
practical_applications: Brand-verified readings for Essilor, Varilux and Comfort Max.
limitations: 2020 release; brand spelling of Varilux varies (ส์ here, ซ์ in Naewna 2019).

title: Naewna lady section: Essilor Varilux 60th anniversary / NEW YEAR NEW YOU campaign
key_findings: Spellings: เอสซีลอร์, วารีลักซ์, เลนส์โปรเกรสซีฟ; website www.essilor.co.th.
practical_applications: Second brand-sourced spelling of Varilux (วารีลักซ์).
limitations: Newspaper reproduction of press content.

title: ZEISS 175 years [PR] (Brand Buffet)
authors: Brand Buffet (PR; quotes MD of Carl Zeiss (Thailand))
key_findings: Body text writes 'ไซส์ส (ZEISS)' and company 'บริษัท คาร์ล ไซส์ส (ประเทศไทย)'; the tag spells 'ไซสส์'.
practical_applications: Brand's Thai written form is ไซส์ส; as TTS input it risks an extra final -t, so a separate spoken respelling is needed.
limitations: Labelled [PR] but issuer not stated explicitly; inconsistent spellings within the page.

title: TH Carl Zeiss General Terms and Conditions (bilingual) - ZEISS asset downloads
key_findings: Per search summary: Thai legal documents name the company 'บริษัท คาร์ล ไซส์ส จำกัด' / 'คาร์ล ไซส์ส (ประเทศไทย)', with a variant 'คารล์ ไซสส์'.
practical_applications: Confirms ZEISS's own Thai form uses ไซส์ส.
limitations: Search summary only; PDF not opened.

title: Daily News article on photochromic ('auto') lenses
key_findings: Body text spells Transitions as 'ทรานซิชั่น' ('เลนส์ทรานซิชั่น', also called 'เลนส์ออโต้'); no brand representative quoted.
practical_applications: Shows common Thai written form; not brand-verified.
limitations: News article, not brand; date not recorded.

title: (How to) อ่านใบตรวจค่าสายตาอย่างไรให้เหมือนผู้เชี่ยวชาญ - หมอแว่น
key_findings: SPH: minus = 'ค่าสายตาสั้น (Myopia)', plus = 'ค่าสายตายาว (Hyperopia)'; unit ไดออปเตอร์.
CYL = 'ค่าสายตาเอียง'; AXIS = 'องศาสายตาเอียง' / 'องศาแกนเอียง'.
ADD = 'ค่า Add', for 'สายตายาวตามวัย (Presbyopia)', +0.75 to +3.00 D.
-2.00 D is 'สายตาสั้นสองจุดศูนย์ไดออปเตอร์' but commonly said 'สั้นสองร้อย'.
practical_applications: Shop VO should say powers in 'hundreds' (สั้นสองร้อย, เอียงเจ็ดสิบห้า) for customers; decimal reading for technical content.
limitations: Practitioner blog of one shop; not an optometry council document.

title: อ่านใบวัดสายตา SPH CYL AXIS ADD PD
url: https://www.putuchon.com/post/อ่านใบวัดสายตา-sph-cyl-axis-add-pd
key_findings: Thai technical glosses: SPH = 'กำลังทรงกลม', CYL = 'กำลังทรงกระบอก', AXIS = 'แกน' (1-180 องศา), ADD = 'กำลังบวกที่เพิ่ม...เพื่อช่วยการมองใกล้', PD = 'ระยะห่างระหว่างรูม่านตาสองข้าง' (มิลลิเมตร).
Minus lens = เลนส์กระจายแสง, plus = เลนส์รวมแสง.
practical_applications: Thai-only glosses for VO when English abbreviations should not be read.
limitations: Practitioner page; no spoken forms given.

title: ทัศนมาตรศาสตร์ - วิกิพีเดีย
url: https://th.wikipedia.org/wiki/ทัศนมาตรศาสตร์
key_findings: Optometry = ทัศนมาตรศาสตร์, a โรคศิลปะ profession; practitioner = 'ผู้ประกอบโรคศิลปะโดยอาศัยทัศนมาตรศาสตร์'.
Cites ประกาศกระทรวงสาธารณสุข ฉบับที่ ๒ (พ.ศ. ๒๕๔๖); mentions ราชวิทยาลัยจักษุแพทย์แห่งประเทศไทย.
practical_applications: Use ทัศนมาตรศาสตร์ / นักทัศนมาตร (common) and จักษุแพทย์ in Thai scripts instead of English.
limitations: Article tagged as needing citations; no council document read.

title: Wiktionary entries: myopia, astigmatism, ophthalmology, titanium, acetate, presbyopia, hyperopia
key_findings: myopia UK /maɪˈəʊ.pɪ.ə/, US /maɪˈoʊ.pi.ə/.
astigmatism US /əˈstɪɡmətɪzm̩/.
ophthalmology UK /ˌɒfθə(l)ˈmɒləd͡ʒi/ ~ /ˌɒpθə(l)ˈmɒləd͡ʒi/; US /ˌɑpθə(l)ˈmɑləd͡ʒi/.
titanium US /taɪˈteɪni.əm/ ~ /tɪˈteɪni.əm/; Thai translation ไทเทเนียม.
acetate /ˈæsɪteɪ̯t/.
presbyopia and hyperopia entries had no English IPA.
practical_applications: English IPA basis for RI-style transcription checks.
limitations: Cambridge and Oxford Learner's dictionaries returned HTTP 403, so the planned Tier-B dictionary IPA could not be read; community source.

title: Thai script - Wikipedia (tone rules section)
key_findings: Class lists: high ข ฃ ฉ ผ ฝ ถ ฐ ศ ษ ส ห; mid ก จ ฎ ฏ ด ต บ ป อ; low = the rest.
Tone table by class x (live / dead short / dead long / mai ek / mai tho / mai tri / mai chattawa).
Low class: dead short → high, dead long → falling.
ห นำ before low sonorants (ง ญ น ม ว ย ร ล); อ นำ only in อย่า อยาก อย่าง อยู่.
practical_applications: Lookup table for checking a TTS tone error against spelling.
limitations: Tone section has no inline citations; first 100k characters read.

title: Creating speech register in Thai conversation
key_findings: Register is built from formality-marking particles, pronouns, names, kin terms, titles and pragmatic particles.
Formality is a matter of degree, from the frequency and combination of these signs.
Strangers in unfamiliar situations negotiate a middle register.
practical_applications: Register in a script is set mainly by particle density, pronoun/kin-term choice and titles, not by vocabulary alone.
Shop VO to unknown customers = middle register (polite particle + kin/title terms, no slang).
limitations: Abstract only; four conversations analysed.

title: Syntactic Distribution and Communicative Function of the /kh/ Polite Particles in Thai
key_findings: Article on distribution and function of ครับ/ค่ะ/คะ-family particles (Language and Linguistics 20(1):11-23).
practical_applications: Key reference to read next for particle placement rules.
limitations: PDF is an image scan without text layer; content not read.

title: The Use of the Thai Final Particle Na by Japanese Learners of Thai
authors: Maklai, Sumintra; Ratitamkul, Theeraporn; Sirikanerat, Thanasak
key_findings: Thai National Corpus: นะ has three functions - softening, emphasising, topic marking.
Native speakers and learners used นะ most for emphasis, least for topic marking.
practical_applications: นะ is not only a softener: placed after a topic ('แว่นตัวนี้นะ ...') it marks the topic - useful for natural VO pacing.
limitations: Abstract only; small pair-discussion sample (10+10).

title: Gender-Differential Tendencies in LINE Use: A Case of Thailand
key_findings: 3,384 LINE messages, 13 colleagues: women used final particles (นะ จ้ะ/จ้า ล่ะ) more; men used more stickers.
คะ/ค่ะ is described as used by females; some men reported using kha playfully/flirtatiously with women.
นะ signals that a response is expected and softens the tone.
Differences are socially constructed and shaped by the platform, not determined by gender alone.
practical_applications: Particle choice signals persona, not just biological sex; avoid stereotyped 'female = many particles' writing.
limitations: One workplace chat group; written chat not speech.

title: Thai sentence particles: forms, meanings and formal-semantic variations (Pacific Linguistics A-80)
key_findings: Foundational description of Thai sentence particles including a chapter on the forms and meanings of นะ (per search summary).
practical_applications: Reference for particle meanings beyond craft knowledge.
limitations: Search summary only; PDF not opened this session.
license: CC BY-SA (Pacific Linguistics open archive) - not checked

title: Thai sentence-final imperative discourse particles (JSEALS 15.1)
key_findings: Per abstract snippet: distribution of imperative particles (incl. นะ) depends on illocutionary force and Searlean felicity conditions.
practical_applications: CTA lines: choose imperative particle by speech act (request vs. suggestion vs. urging).
limitations: Search summary only; author name as shown by search, not confirmed on the article page.

title: ระดับภาษาและการใช้ภาษาที่ถูกต้อง (course 113-108 การใช้ภาษาไทยเพื่อการสื่อสาร, week 3)
authors: อ.รักษ์พงศ์ ธรรมผุสนา, Siam University
key_findings: Register = gradation of wording chosen by occasion, relationship and content.
Formal: พิธีการ (ceremony, high literature) and ทางการ/มาตรฐานราชการ (official letters, theses, speeches).
Informal: กึ่งทางการ (polite but not strict; business, people one does not know well or who are older/senior, lectures, light writing) and สนทนา / กันเอง levels.
practical_applications: Shop VO and ads sit at กึ่งทางการ; Mint & Tao dialogue at สนทนา/กันเอง.
limitations: Teaching handout (2011 semester 1/2554); school-grammar taxonomy, not sociolinguistic research.

title: Roles of English in facial cosmetic advertisements in Thai magazines
key_findings: In 100 Thai cosmetic print ads, English is 'not really used for presenting meaning' but to catch attention, enhance product image/value and signal modernity.
practical_applications: English brand/tech words in our ads work as image signals - keep them few and say them clearly; carry the actual message in Thai.
limitations: Abstract only; print ads, one product category.

title: Thai-English Code Mixing and Code Switching in Cosmopolitan Magazine
key_findings: Intrasentential code mixing was the most frequent; no tag switching found (per search snippet).
practical_applications: Thai copy typically mixes single English words inside Thai sentences - the case TTS handles worst.
limitations: Search summary only.

title: Linguistic Devices in Digital Tourism Advertisements by the Tourism Authority of Thailand (TAT): A Discourse Analysis Perspective
key_findings: 30 TAT digital ads (Facebook, web, YouTube, 2022-2025): lexical selection ~42.5%, speech acts ~17.5%, claiming ~9.9% of devices.
Four strategies: creating atmosphere/identity, directing action, establishing credibility/authority, framing perspectives.
practical_applications: Ad script checklist: one mood/identity line, one clear action line, one credibility line.
limitations: Abstract only; tourism, not retail optics.

title: Socio-cultural factors influencing face manifestation and communicative behaviour in Thai service encounters
key_findings: เกรงใจ (consideration for others) is a key factor in Thai service communication.
Role/socio-economic differences between agents and customers shape communication; agents' customer-facing face can conflict with organisational face.
practical_applications: Shop VO should leave the customer room to decide (no hard push); offers phrased as invitations.
limitations: Abstract only; hotel/travel settings.

title: Understanding Elderspeak: An Evolutionary Concept Analysis (Innovation in Aging)
key_findings: Per search summary: studies disagree whether elderspeak helps or hinders comprehension; exaggerated prosody reduces comprehension.
Elderspeak is generally perceived as patronising; in dementia it increases resistiveness to care.
practical_applications: For older customers: slower, clearer and well-paced speech is fine; sing-song exaggerated pitch and baby-talk terms are not.
limitations: Search summary only (PMC page blocked by bot check); Western care settings; authors not recorded.

title: The text analysis and processing of Thai language text to speech conversion system
key_findings: Thai texts often contain numbers, abbreviations and currency symbols; the two core problems are detecting non-standard words and disambiguating their reading.
practical_applications: Normaliser needs context rules (e.g. 6/6 vision vs 6/6 date).
limitations: Abstract-level record via search only.

title: JaiTTS: A Thai Voice Cloning Model
authors: Karnjanaekarin, J.; Trakuekul, P.; Panitsrisit, N.; Sumanakul, S.; Nitayasomboon, V.; Guntasin, N.; Denkavin, T.; Rutherford, A. T.
key_findings: Handles numerals and Thai-English code-switching without explicit text normalisation.
Short-utterance CER 1.94% vs human ground truth 1.98%; won 283 / lost 58 of 400 pairwise comparisons against commercial systems.
practical_applications: Modern end-to-end TTS can read raw numbers, but explicit normalisation stays the safe default for prices, powers and dates whose reading is a choice (casual vs formal).
limitations: Preprint abstract only; normalisation errors by category not reported in the abstract.

title: Empowering Global Voices: A Data-Efficient, Phoneme-Tone Adaptive Approach to High-Fidelity Speech Synthesis
authors: Geng, Yizhong; Xu, Jizhuo; Liang, Zeyu; Yang, Jinghan; Shi, Xiaoyi; Shen, Xiaoyu
key_findings: Uses Thai as a case study where 'intricate phonetic rules and sparse resources' are addressed via a phoneme-tone adaptive approach; claims state-of-the-art subjective/objective scores.
practical_applications: Confirms that tone-aware G2P is a known Thai TTS weak point; keep respellings that force tones.
limitations: Abstract only; details of preprocessing not read.

title: Exploring Patterns and Challenges in English Word-Final Consonant Pronunciation among Southern Thai EFL Learners
key_findings: Per search summary: 27 undergraduates often dropped English final stops; voiced finals most often mispronounced or omitted; linked to Thai/Southern Thai phonology.
practical_applications: English lines for Thai staff: mark final consonants (price, size, fifty/fifteen) and drill them; avoid words ending in clusters where a simpler word exists.
limitations: Search summary only; small sample; year not confirmed.

title: Metric Units and Everyday Measures (Thai grammar page)
key_findings: Per search summary: ครึ่งลิตร = half a litre; สองลิตรครึ่ง = two and a half litres (ครึ่ง after the unit adds a half).
practical_applications: Normaliser rule: N.5 + unit → N + unit + ครึ่ง (casual).
limitations: Search summary only; site of unknown authority. Needs a reference grammar check.

title: Politeness and pragmatic competence in Thai speakers of English (Newcastle University PhD thesis)
key_findings: Per search summary: for Thai hotel workers speaking English, negative politeness was the chosen strategy in most scenarios.
practical_applications: English staff scripts: indirect, option-giving phrasing feels natural to Thai staff.
limitations: Search summary only; title and author inferred from the file name and snippet, not confirmed.
